content: While bloating and abdominal distension can be symptoms of underlying organic diseases, the most common cause is constipation. Other potential causes include irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), gastroparesis, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), and certain gynecological conditions. The exact mechanisms behind bloating are not fully understood, but proposed causes include visceral hypersensitivity, abnormal abdominal wall-diaphragmatic reflexes, poor digestion of fermentable carbohydrates, and alterations in the gut microbiome. A thorough medical history and physical examination are essential for evaluation, with a focus on ruling out organic disorders. Management strategies typically involve dietary changes, behavioral therapy, microbiome modulation, and medical treatments. Historically, bloating has been described in various ways. In 1891, Bernheim documented a woman who likened her symptoms to going up and down like an accordion. In 1900, Kaplan referred to ventre en accordéon and noted that in cases of suspected intestinal obstruction, puncturing the intestines revealed no gas in cases of hysterical bloating. Bloating was also once considered a tumor that disappeared under anesthesia and reappeared when the patient regained consciousness. In 1884, Krukenberg associated bloating with lordosis, and in 1949, Alvarez of the Mayo Clinic described bloating in a woman with psychiatric issues. There is no universally accepted classification system for bloating. However, several mechanisms have been proposed to explain its pathophysiology: 1. Abnormal Gut Microbiota: The composition of colonic microflora and the types of gas they produce are linked to bloating. Methanogenic flora, in particular, has been implicated. Studies have shown that individuals with low methane production experience more bloating after consuming sorbitol and fiber compared to high methane producers. 2. Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): Bacterial fermentation in the small intestine can lead to gas production, contributing to bloating in patients with IBS. 3. Intestinal Gas Accumulation: Increased intestinal gas levels are associated with bloating. For example, after a large meal, postprandial gas volume in the pelvic colon can increase by 65%. During fasting, the gastrointestinal tract produces approximately 100 mL of gas, which is distributed throughout the digestive system. 4. Altered Gut Motility: Disorders affecting gut motility, such as intestinal dysmotility, can impair the clearance of gas from the gastrointestinal tract, both during fasting and after meals. 5. Abnormal Abdominal-Diaphragmatic Reflexes: Abnormalities in the reflexes involving the abdominal wall and diaphragm, such as increased anterior wall tone and diaphragm relaxation, have been observed in individuals with bloating. 6. Visceral Hypersensitivity: Patients with functional gastrointestinal disorders may perceive normal stimuli or small variations in gas content as bloating. The autonomic nervous system may also play a role, as sympathetic activation can heighten the perception of intestinal distension. 7. Food Intolerance and Carbohydrate Malabsorption: Diets high in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPs) can lead to prolonged hydrogen production, colonic distension, increased fluid delivery to the colon, and gastrointestinal symptoms. 8. Constipation: Retained feces in the rectum can alter gut motility and increase bacterial fermentation, contributing to bloating. The most common causes of bloating include constipation, pregnancy, IBS, celiac disease, carbohydrate intolerances (e.g., lactose or fructose), pancreatic insufficiency, gastroparesis, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, scleroderma, chronic idiopathic pseudo-obstruction, SIBO, acute gastroenteritis, gastric or ovarian malignancies, and ascites. Bloating must be differentiated from other conditions, such as lactose or fructose intolerance, celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, IBS, functional dyspepsia, functional bloating, constipation, diabetes, scleroderma, pseudo-obstruction, gastroparesis, ileus, gastric outlet obstruction, small bowel obstruction, superior mesenteric artery syndrome, colonic obstruction, volvulus, gastrointestinal or ovarian malignancies, ascites, pregnancy, and obesity. In the United States, 15-30% of the general population reports experiencing bloating. A telephone survey found a prevalence of 16% among adults who reported bloating or distension in the past month. Women are more likely than men to report bloating, and there is no racial predilection. Risk factors for bloating include behaviors that increase air swallowing, such as chewing gum, consuming hard candy, or drinking carbonated beverages. Certain foods, such as leafy greens, beans, bran, and dairy products, can also contribute to bloating, particularly in individuals with lactose intolerance. Routine screening for bloating is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. While bloating is often attributed to excessive gas, the relationship between gas volume and symptoms is unclear. Chronic bloating may result from heightened sensitivity to gas or exaggerated motor responses to normal gas levels. Bloating-related pain is typically sharp, cramp-like, and may shift locations. Although bloating is usually benign, it can occasionally indicate serious conditions, such as intestinal obstruction or malignancy. The diagnosis of functional bloating is based on the Rome IV criteria, which require recurrent bloating or distension at least one day per week for at least three months, with symptom onset at least six months prior to diagnosis. Symptoms must not meet the criteria for IBS, functional constipation, functional diarrhea, or postprandial distress syndrome. A detailed history should include the onset of symptoms, dietary triggers (e.g., wheat, dairy, fructose, fiber, nonabsorbable sugars), diurnal variation, and associated symptoms such as constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or postprandial fullness. Functional bloating often follows a diurnal pattern, worsening after meals and improving overnight. Physical examination findings may include abdominal distension and altered bowel sounds. Alarm features, such as occult fecal blood, skin changes (e.g., sclerodactyly in scleroderma, dermatitis herpetiformis in celiac disease), neuropathy, cachexia, jaundice, or palpable masses, suggest an underlying organic disease. Laboratory tests may include a complete blood count to evaluate for anemia, serologies for celiac disease (e.g., anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, endomysial antibodies, deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies), hydrogen breath tests for SIBO and lactose intolerance, thyroid function tests, fasting cortisol levels, and antibody tests for collagen vascular diseases or paraneoplastic visceral neuropathy. Stool analysis may include antigen testing for Giardia. Imaging studies, such as abdominal X-rays, ultrasounds, or CT scans, may be used to rule out intestinal obstruction, ascites, or ovarian cancer. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is indicated for alarm features, such as weight loss, abdominal pain, dysphagia, heartburn, or regurgitation. Treatment involves patient education, dietary modifications, and behavioral therapy. Patients should minimize air swallowing by avoiding gum chewing, smoking, carbonated beverages, and rapid consumption of food or liquids. For refractory symptoms, baclofen (10 mg three times daily) may reduce transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations and suppress swallowing rates, thereby decreasing belching. Surgery is not recommended for bloating management.
